tier_reason: The blog is a single-author personal experiment (one run each), not peer-reviewed and not an established third-party suite. Its scripts are public (rnk/llvm-nativelink-demo build-llvm-recc/reconfig.sh: CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, /opt/llvm clang, PCH disabled), but no CPU model is given for the laptop or the cluster nodes, so it is not A, and a one-off blog falls to C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Independent blog (Reid Kleckner, 2026-03-30): a full LLVM + Clang build with CMake/Ninja took 1026.169s locally on the author's laptop (Ninja default -j, no remote execution, PCH disabled) vs 257.527s distributed through recc + NativeLink at -j96 over WiFi, about 4.0x (the intro says 'four times faster than my laptop, going from 1026s to 253s'). With PCH enabled, the local build took 682.778s, and the author writes that 'the distributed build is only 2.65x faster than the local build', calling the 4x an 'overstatement'. In the recc build directory, a clean rebuild with a full cache hit rate took 92.885s vs 266.600s for the preceding cold build (over VPN). NativeLink's homepage separately claims '4-15x faster builds' demonstrated on LLVM, with no methodology.
corrections.hardware: Client: the author's laptop (model and CPU not stated), over WiFi (the cache test was over a VPN). Remote: a home Kubernetes cluster on Talos Linux made of small, low-power control nodes plus extra unpictured nodes; the author says his Framework desktop 'is doing most of the heavy lifting'. No CPU models are stated.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Toolchain from LLVM's ghcr.io/llvm/ci-ubuntu-24.04 container (LTO/BOLT-optimized clang); CMake + Ninja with recc as the compiler launcher; the linked demo repo's reconfig.sh uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, LLVM_TARGETS_TO_BUILD=X86, CMAKE_DISABLE_PRECOMPILE_HEADERS=ON; distributed run at -j96, local run at Ninja's default -j
corrections.caveats: Single-author personal experiment, one run per configuration, by an independent LLVM/Clang contributor. It compares a laptop against a laptop plus a remote cluster (mostly a Framework desktop), not against distcc, icecc or ccache. The author concedes the 4x headline is an overstatement: with PCH enabled locally the gain is 2.65x, because recc could not handle PCH. No CPU models are given. NativeLink's '4-15x' homepage figure has no published methodology. License is FSL-1.1-Apache-2.0 (not OSI; each release converts to Apache-2.0 after two years).

notes: The record's hardware was wrong: the laptop was the client, the Framework desktop was a cluster worker, and 'OptiBlex' nodes do not appear on the page. The 'LLVM builds 4 times faster ... 17 minutes to 4' vendor quote was not found; the homepage says '4-15x faster builds'. GitHub reports license NOASSERTION; LICENSE is FSL-1.1-Apache-2.0, so 'reference' is correct.

tier_reason: The features page gives first-party round numbers ('Caching can accelerate compile times up to 10x', Unity/Blob 'Improvements of 10x or more are not uncommon', distributed 'Speedups of 5x are common') relative to building without those features. It gives no workload, hardware, compiler, flags or code, so these are numbers without methodology.

corrections.baseline: the same build without FASTBuild's object cache, Unity/Blob builds or distributed compilation (implicit; no baseline tool is named)
corrections.caveats: No baseline tool (ccache/sccache/distcc/IncrediBuild) is named. The figures are unqualified marketing-style numbers with no workload, hardware, compiler or flags. The Unity/Blob gain comes from the unity-build technique itself, which other build systems also offer. The page's comparisons with Visual Studio/MSBuild, make and SCons are qualitative only. GitHub reports no license because the license file is at Code/LICENSE.TXT (zlib license text).

notes: All three quoted figures appear verbatim on the features page. The default branch 'main' was last committed 2026-07-26; the 'dev' branch (where patches land) was last committed 2026-09-20, which matches the record, so last_commit was left unchanged. Code/LICENSE.TXT is the zlib license text with an added attribution example, so Zlib/copyable stands.

tier_reason: The README chart (assets/compilation_times.png) is first-party and compares homcc against distcc directly on an internal Celonis codebase with clang++-14. It gives no hardware, no benchmark script and no raw data, so it is C.

corrections.workload: Distributed remote compilation of a Celonis-internal C++ codebase with clang++-14 (total server job limit 112, 60 compilation threads), measuring total remote compilation time at up/download bandwidths from 5/25 Mbps to 1000/1000 Mbps, comparing homcc vs. distcc.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark uses an internal, non-public Celonis C++ codebase, so it cannot be reproduced independently. The only numbers are in a chart image, with no CPU model, raw data or benchmark script. Values were read off the bar chart and are approximate. The README text claims compilation times 'smaller by some orders of magnitudes' on small uplinks, but its own chart shows at most about 6x, and distcc is slightly faster at 1000/1000 Mbps.

notes: I opened the chart image; the bar readings in claimed_speedup match (about 9.2 vs 57.6 min at 5/25 Mbps, about 5.8 vs 5.0 min at 1000/1000). The README does not say the bandwidths were simulated, so that word was removed from workload. Metadata (MIT, 24 stars, last commit 2026-08-18) is correct.

tier_reason: The README #benchmark table is first-party and compares 'Without octobuild' against octobuild at 0% and 100% cache. CPUs are named and MSVC 2019 is named for Win64, but flags are not stated and the game project is unnamed, so it is not reproducible. The builds are DebugGame configurations.

corrections.baseline: stock Unreal Build Tool / Unreal Automation Tool build without octobuild (README 'Without octobuild' column)
corrections.claimed_speedup: README states octobuild reduces re-compile time 'by 60-90%'. Benchmark table at 100% cache hit vs. without octobuild: Linux 3m54s to 36s (~6.5x), Win64 8m4s to 2m15s (~3.6x), PS4 6m12s to 2m34s (~2.4x), PS5 5m48s to 2m11s (~2.7x), XB1 4m40s to 1m39s (~2.8x), XSX 4m49s to 1m40s (~2.9x) (derived from page data). With a cold (0%) cache octobuild is equal or slower: Linux 3m53s, Win64 10m6s, PS4 7m10s, PS5 6m56s, XB1 6m10s, XSX 5m42s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Win64: MSVC 2019 (stated); Linux and console toolchains not named; UE 5.0.3 DebugGame configuration via RunUAT.sh (Linux) and RunUBT.bat (Win64, consoles); compiler flags not stated
corrections.workload: Build of an unnamed Unreal Engine 5.0.3 game project (<game>Editor DebugGame for Linux and Win64, <game> DebugGame for PS4, PS5, Xbox One and Xbox Series X), comparing no octobuild vs. octobuild with a cold (0%) and a fully warm (100%) cache.
corrections.caveats: No comparison with other caches or accelerators (ccache, sccache, distcc, IncrediBuild) appears in the README; the only baseline is a build without octobuild. The numbers are first-party, from an unnamed game project, with no published harness and no compiler flags; builds are DebugGame. On a cold cache octobuild is up to about 25% slower (Win64 10m6s vs 8m4s).

notes: All table values match the README exactly. The record's claims that consoles use 'platform-bundled clang' and that ccache/distcc cannot support MSVC do not appear on the page, so they were removed. Metadata (MIT, 285 stars, last commit 2026-09-15) is correct.

tier_reason: Two independent third-party sources show zapcc beating GCC and Clang on compile time. The Wicht blog tables match the record but give no CPU model or flags. Colfax Research's 2017 compiler comparison (Table 1: TMV compile 510 s Zapcc 1.0.1 vs 848 s G++ 7.2.0 and 902 s Clang 5.0.0, on a 2-socket Xeon Platinum 8168) supports B. It is not A because the TMV compile flags are not stated and its TMV build is not in ColfaxResearch/CompilerComparisonCode.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.4.0, Clang 3.9, zapcc++ (beta); ETL debug and release configurations; optimization flags not stated on the page
corrections.workload: Full build of the ETL (Expression Template Library, header-only, template-heavy) test cases: debug at -j1/-j2/-j4, release at -j1 only; link time excluded
corrections.caveats: The blog benchmark (2016) predates modern GCC/Clang by many major versions and states no CPU model or flags. The biggest gains are on debug builds (3.3x vs Clang, about 2x vs GCC); release gains are 1.5x/1.2x. Corroboration: Colfax Research 'A Performance-Based Comparison of C/C++ Compilers' (2017-11-11) Table 1 gives TMV library compile times of 510 s for Zapcc 1.0.1 vs 848 s for G++ 7.2.0 and 902 s for Clang 5.0.0 (~1.66x/~1.77x, derived from page data) on a 2-socket Xeon Platinum 8168. The -O3 -march=skylake-avx512 lines in that paper are for the compute kernels, not the TMV compile. The project has been abandoned since 2020 (last merged with LLVM trunk 2018-02-13). GitHub reports license NOASSERTION; LICENSE.TXT is the LLVM Release License (University of Illinois/NCSA).

notes: All blog numbers match exactly (debug -j1 469/710/214 s; release -j1 782/960/640 s). The release build was measured at -j1 only, not -j1/-j2/-j4. I confirmed the Colfax per-compiler figures directly from its Table 1. If a single URL with a CPU model is preferred, https://colfaxresearch.com/compiler-comparison/ is the stronger B source.
